questions.question: 1. For an 'uplink' SINR calculation, what is the 'desired signal'?

answers.a: The signal from the base station, received at the mobile phone.
answers.b: The signal from the mobile phone, received at its serving base station.
answers.c: The signal from an interfering mobile phone.
answers.d: The noise at the mobile phone's receiver.

questions.question: 2. What is the primary source of 'interference' in an uplink SINR calculation?

answers.a: Signals from co-channel base stations received at the mobile phone.
answers.b: Signals from other mobile phones in other cells (using the same frequency) received at the serving base station.
answers.c: Noise at the serving base station's receiver.
answers.d: The serving base station's own transmitted signal.

questions.question: 3. Where is the 'noise' component measured or considered in an uplink SINR calculation?

answers.b: In the air between the phone and the base station.
answers.d: At the interfering mobile phone's receiver.

questions.question: 4. How does a base station's antenna downtilt affect the *uplink*?

answers.a: It only affects the downlink; it has no effect on the uplink.
answers.b: It changes the transmit power of the mobile phone.
answers.c: It changes the gain of the base station's antenna for receiving signals from different vertical angles.
answers.d: It changes the frequency the mobile phone uses.

questions.question: 5. If a base station *increases* its downtilt, what is the likely effect on the received signal from an *interfering* mobile phone located very far away?

answers.a: The interfering signal strength will increase.
answers.b: The interfering signal strength will be unaffected.
answers.c: The interfering signal strength will decrease, as it is now outside the antenna's main reception lobe.

questions.question: 6. A mobile user is at the far edge of their cell. If the serving base station applies *excessive* downtilt, what might happen to the *uplink* signal from this user?

answers.a: The base station will receive the signal much more strongly.
answers.b: The base station will receive the signal more weakly, as the user is no longer in the main reception lobe.
answers.c: The mobile phone will transmit with less power.
answers.d: The interference from other cells will be zero.

questions.question: 7. What is the main benefit of using antenna downtilt for *uplink* performance?

answers.a: It increases the signal received from every mobile phone, no matter how far.
answers.b: It reduces interference received from distant co-channel mobile phones, improving the uplink SINR.
answers.c: It eliminates all background noise at the base station.
answers.d: It allows the mobile phone to use less battery power.

questions.question: 8. An interfering mobile phone (in another cell) moves *closer* to *your* serving base station. What happens to your uplink SINR?

answers.a: It increases, because your desired signal gets stronger.
answers.c: It decreases, because the interfering signal received at your base station gets stronger.
answers.d: It decreases, because the noise level increases.

questions.question: 9. A base station antenna with *no* downtilt (or even uptilt) would be more susceptible to what problem in the uplink?

answers.a: Receiving too much noise from the ground.
answers.b: Being unable to receive signals from users directly under the tower.
answers.c: Receiving strong interference from very distant mobile phones in co-channel cells.
answers.d: Having its signal blocked by buildings.

questions.question: 10. In the context of uplink SINR, 'power control' is often used. What is the goal of power control for a mobile phone?

answers.a: To transmit with maximum power at all times to ensure the strongest signal.
answers.b: To adjust its transmit power so the base station receives an adequate signal, without causing excessive interference to other cells.
answers.c: To turn off its transmitter to save battery.
answers.d: To match the transmit power of the base station.
